notes: New domain added to the corpus (economics, previously absent). Class B document (14 units). Covers supply/demand curves and equilibrium. One ECU for the worked example.

units.label: Hook: concert ticket prices (text)
units.content_summary: Why do concert tickets for a popular artist cost $200 while a local band's show costs $10? The answer lies in supply and demand — the two forces that determine prices in a market economy.

units.label: Learning Objectives (text)
units.content_summary: Objectives: define supply and demand; read supply and demand curves; identify market equilibrium; explain what happens when supply or demand shifts.

units.label: Demand definition and law (text)
units.content_summary: Demand is the quantity of a good buyers are willing to purchase at various prices. The Law of Demand: as price increases, quantity demanded decreases (all else equal) — buyers want more of something when it's cheaper.

units.label: Demand curve diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Downward-sloping demand curve on a price (y-axis) vs quantity (x-axis) graph, showing that as price falls, quantity demanded rises.

units.label: Supply definition and law (text)
units.content_summary: Supply is the quantity of a good sellers are willing to produce at various prices. The Law of Supply: as price increases, quantity supplied increases (all else equal) — sellers want to produce more when they can earn more per unit.

units.label: Supply curve diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Upward-sloping supply curve on the same price vs quantity graph, showing that as price rises, quantity supplied rises.

units.label: Market equilibrium (text)
units.content_summary: Equilibrium occurs where the supply and demand curves intersect — the price at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded. At this point, there is no surplus (excess supply) or shortage (excess demand).

units.label: Combined supply-demand graph (image)
units.content_summary: Both curves plotted on the same graph, intersecting at the equilibrium point, with equilibrium price and quantity labeled on the axes.

units.label: Worked example: concert tickets (text)
units.content_summary: Applying the model to the opening hook: a popular artist has low supply (limited venue seats) and high demand (many fans), pushing equilibrium price up to $200. The local band has similar supply but far lower demand, so equilibrium price is only $10.

units.label: Worked example graph comparison (image)
units.content_summary: Two side-by-side supply-demand graphs: one for the popular artist (demand curve far right, high equilibrium price) and one for the local band (demand curve near origin, low equilibrium price).

units.label: Shifts in supply and demand (text)
units.content_summary: External factors shift entire curves (not just movement along them): increased income shifts demand right; a new competitor shifts supply right. A shift changes the equilibrium price and quantity.

units.label: Practice problems (text)
units.content_summary: Four problems: identify whether a scenario shifts supply or demand; predict the effect on equilibrium price; read equilibrium price/quantity off a given graph; explain a real-world price change using the model.
